chunks: "PPA is power, performance and area, the three numbers you trade against each other in chip design.
Performance is how fast the thing does its job, so clock speed, instructions per cycle, throughput.
Power is how much energy it burns, which is the switching power, alpha C V squared f, plus leakage.
Area is how much silicon it uses, which really means cost, because bigger dies yield worse and fit fewer per wafer. The trade-offs are everywhere.
If I want more speed I can raise voltage, but power goes up with V squared on top of the frequency, so you pay roughly cubically.
I can deepen the pipeline to raise the clock, which costs flop area and clock power. I can add parallel units or a bigger cache to raise throughput, which costs area and leakage.
I can use low-threshold-voltage cells on critical paths, which are faster but leak more.
And I can go the other way, relaxing the clock target so synthesis uses smaller, slower, lower-power cells. Which corner you pick depends on the product.
A phone SoC cares about power and area. A server CPU pays area and power for performance.
A tiny IoT sensor wants minimum area and almost no power, and it doesn't care how slow it is."
